conceptTag: A complaint about you goes viral
readerTitle: Your company is trending, and not in a good way
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (가정 수리 서비스 회사의 고객지원팀) + 서비스 회복 역설 관련 실제 연구 언급
insight: 바이럴 불만은 평판 문제가 아니라 고객 여정의 한 단계가 고장 났다는 신호다. 공개 대응보다 그 단계를 고치는 것이 진짜 해결이다.
misconception: 바이럴 불만은 홍보 위기이니 사실관계를 먼저 따지고, 게시물을 내리게 하거나 책임자를 징계하면 끝난다.

sources.text: de Matos, C. A., Henrique, J. L., & Rossi, C. A. V. (2007). Service Recovery Paradox: A Meta-Analysis. Journal of Service Research.
McCollough, M. A., Berry, L. L., & Yadav, M. S. (2000). An Empirical Investigation of Customer Satisfaction After Service Failure and Recovery. Journal of Service Research.
시나리오의 회사, 고객, 수치는 모두 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: 7번 카드의 연구 요약(메타분석에서 회복 후 만족도는 오를 수 있으나 재구매 의도·충성도에서는 효과가 약하거나 나타나지 않음)을 de Matos et al.(2007) 원문으로 확인하세요.
"첫 번째의 비교적 가벼운 실패를 아주 잘 회복했을 때 주로 나타난다"는 조건 요약이 McCollough et al.(2000) 등 선행 연구와 일치하는지 확인하세요.
시나리오 수치(기술자 약 40명, 지난 한 달 미청취 메시지 20여 건, 바닥 건조 비용 수백 달러)는 모두 가상입니다.

cards.title: Your company is trending, and not in a good way
body: Saturday, 9:40 p.m. You lead the customer care team at a home repair company with about 40 technicians.
A customer has posted a video in a big local community group: water across her kitchen floor, one day after your plumber fixed a leak. *"Called them three times. Nobody called back."*
By Sunday morning it has hundreds of comments and is spreading well beyond the group.

image.label: Phone screen showing a flooded kitchen post with many comments
image.brief: 어두운 거실에서 빛나는 스마트폰 화면. 물이 고인 부엌 사진이 올라간 게시물 아래로 댓글과 공유 아이콘 숫자가 계속 늘어나는 느낌. 실제 SNS 로고나 UI는 쓰지 말고 가상의 커뮤니티 앱으로.

cards.title: What do you do first?
body: It's Sunday morning. You don't know the full story yet, and the technician is off until Monday.

options.text: Reply publicly now: apologize that she was left waiting, say you're calling her today, then call
options.feedback: You give up checking every fact first, but everyone watching sees someone is listening. The part that matters most, that nobody called back, is already true.

options.text: Message her privately to sort it out, without replying in public
options.feedback: Fixing it one-to-one is right. But under a growing post, the public still sees only silence.

options.text: Wait until you've spoken to the technician on Monday
options.feedback: You avoid saying something wrong, but a day of silence lets the post tell the story. It looks exactly like the non-response she complained about.

cards.title: Say you replied and called. What do you offer?
body: On the phone she's calmer than her post. A fitting under the sink failed overnight. Her three calls went to a weekend voicemail box nobody checks. A floor-drying service quoted her a few hundred dollars.

options.text: Send the on-call plumber today, waive the bill and pay for the drying
options.feedback: It costs more than a warranty fix. It also solves her whole problem today, which is what she expected the first time.

options.text: Book a free warranty repair for the first open slot, on Wednesday
options.feedback: Fair by the policy, but it repeats the original failure: she waits again, with a wet floor.

options.text: Offer a large voucher for future work
options.feedback: Generous, but it asks her to trust you with more work before this problem is fixed.

cards.title: The floor is dry. The post is still up.
body: The repair is done Sunday evening. She thanks you and says she'll update her post. Your marketing manager has ideas too.

options.text: With her okay, post a short follow-up: what went wrong, what you fixed, what you'll change
options.feedback: Owning it in public invites a few more critics. It also turns the thread into proof of how you act when things go wrong.

options.text: Ask her to delete the post now that it's resolved
options.feedback: If she shares that request, it becomes the new story. And people who saw the complaint never see the fix.

options.text: Let her update speak for itself and say nothing more
options.feedback: Her words carry more weight than yours. But readers are still waiting to hear what you'll change.

cards.title: Monday morning. What do you fix?
body: Your operations director wants the technician disciplined. Failed fittings are rare. The voicemail box is not: you find about two dozen unheard weekend messages from the past month.

options.text: Discipline the technician so everyone sees it was taken seriously
options.feedback: It looks decisive but changes nothing. Next weekend, a caller still reaches a box nobody checks.

options.text: Route after-hours calls to the on-call plumber and track every callback until it's closed
options.feedback: It costs on-call time and a new routine. It fixes the step that turned a normal repair problem into a public one.

options.text: Remind all technicians to double-check fittings
options.feedback: Sensible, but it targets the rare failure, not the common one.

cards.softwareNote: In software, the weekend voicemail box is often a support form that auto-replies, then sits in a queue nobody owns, or a ticket closed automatically after a few days.

cards.eyebrow: What the post was really about
cards.title: The leak wasn't the story. The silence was.
body: Repairs fail sometimes, and customers often accept that. What made her angry was three unanswered calls when she needed you most.
That callback was a **moment of truth**: a point in the journey where the customer decides whether you can be trusted. The post simply showed thousands of people a broken step in your journey.

image.label: Customer journey line with one broken step highlighted
image.brief: 고객 여정 타임라인 인포그래픽. "Booking", "Repair", "Problem returns", "Calls for help", "Callback" 순서. "Callback" 단계만 끊어진 선과 빨간색으로 강조하고, 그 위에 작은 확성기 아이콘.

cards.title: A great recovery isn't a free pass.
body: The **service recovery paradox** is the idea that a well-handled failure can leave customers happier than no failure at all. Research is mixed. A meta-analysis found satisfaction can rise after a strong recovery, but loyalty and repurchase intentions often don't.
It tends to work only for a first, fairly minor failure. If the same thing happens twice, it stops working.
And some viral posts are unfair. If facts are wrong, correct them once, calmly, without attacking the customer.

cards.title: A viral complaint is a broken step, told in public.
body: Each decision used an idea from this unit:
list: **Reply fast:** moments of truth. People judge you by what you do when it counts.
**Fix it fully:** expectations vs experience. Deliver what she expected the first time.
**Close the loop in public:** service as marketing. The fix is an ad, too.
**Fix the callback step:** the customer journey and consistency. Repair the process, not the person.
cards.callout: **Try it today:** call your own after-hours line or send your support form tonight. See how long the answer takes.
